"If I have to listen to one more lecture on the intricacies of mana efficiency, I might actually explode."

The voice that drifted from behind me was not the trembling plea of a first-year student, but a low, melodic hum that vibrated through my very bones. I did not turn around. I knew that tone. It belonged to anyone who had lived a thousand years within the crushing pressure of a dark throne room and were now forced to endure the fluorescent lights of St. Celestia Academy’s Advanced Spellcasting Department.

My name is Soren Wade, and I am currently labeled by the school’s administrative staff as "Subject Zero: Dangerously Inefficient."

Being an isekai protagonist usually means being chosen by a goddess, handed a holy sword, or granted overwhelming magical power. I got none of those things. Instead, I received a faint, golden spark upon arriving in this new world, which they mistook for "potential" but I knew was simply the lingering energy from my previous life as the Archdemon Malphas, the most feared ruler of the Abyssal Plains.

While others in my class—cute girls with ribbons in their hair and boys with endless enthusiasm—wrestled with basic fireballs and wind charms, I sat staring at my quill. To them, magic was about elegance. To me, it was about control. I wasn't just failing to cast; I was rejecting their rigid, structured system of magic because it felt like trying to pour water into a square hole.

"Soren-san! You aren't even looking at the chalkboard!" a bright voice chirped.

It was Chiyo-sama, a prodigy whose mana pool was so vast she could accidentally vaporize a mountain range if she sneezed too hard. She floated over, her wings shimmering with iridescent light. "The instructor, Professor Hestia-sensei, is giving a special tutorial on high-density etheric weaving today! Isn't this exciting? We could be making enchanted armor soon!"

I sighed, closing my eyes. The classroom was a chaotic sea of movement. Students were sparring gently, laughing at each other’s failed attempts at illusions, and generally behaving like humans enjoying a summer afternoon. It made my stomach ache. This was exactly what I wanted. No wars, no demon slayers, no endless bloodbaths. Just peace. Just books. Just retirement.

But peace doesn't come easily when you’re a walking catastrophe.

The bell rang, signaling the start of the practical exam. Professor Hestia-sensei, a stern woman with silver hair tied back in a severe bun, stood before us. Her eyes scanned the room, landing on me last. A frown touched her lips.

"Wade-kun," she called out. "As the designated demonstration candidate, you will attempt to weave a basic barrier spell. Show us why your record shows 'unstable'... and disastrous."

A murmur went through the class. Even Chiyo-sama looked concerned. Unstable? Disastrous? They couldn't see the truth. They saw a boy who kept accidentally turning his potion ingredients into frogs or setting off sparks instead of flames. They didn't realize I was just holding back. If I used even a fraction of my actual power—the kind that could level a city block—I wouldn't just fail; I would break the academy's foundation.

I stepped forward, feeling the weight of fifty pairs of eyes. The air in the room grew heavy with anticipation. My heart, however, remained calm. I closed my eyes and reached inward, past the shallow pools of human mana, toward the deep, roaring abyss where my true strength slept.

Focus, I told myself. One small spark.

I began the incantation, my voice low and steady. As I channeled mana into my hands, the air around me began to crackle with violet lightning. The students gasped.

"Too much, Soren-san!" someone whispered.

I ignored them. I had spent centuries mastering the art of suppression. I pushed the mana into the air, forcing it into the shape of a barrier. But my control slipped. Not because I was weak, but because I was tired. I was exhausted from pretending to be something I was no longer.

Instead of a graceful dome of translucent blue light, a massive pillar of jagged, crimson energy erupted from my fingertips. It wasn't a shield; it was a wall of pure, terrifying pressure. The shockwave blew the doors off the training room and sent papers flying. The ground trembled. The violet aura flared, casting long, dancing shadows against the stone walls.

Silence descended, thick and suffocating.

Then, I heard a soft crash from the corner of the room. My hand had knocked over the table near the window. Through the glass, I saw a small bird fly away, terrified. I winced. That was all I really cared about right now.

"Stop," I whispered.

The crimson pillar didn't just collapse; it imploded with a roar that sounded like the end of the world. The sheer force sucked the oxygen out of the room, leaving everyone coughing and dazed. When the dust settled, there was no pillar. There was only me, standing in the center of a crater, holding a single, ordinary feather that had drifted down from the ceiling.

Professor Hestia-sensei stared at me, her face pale. "That... that was not a barrier. That was a localized reality fracture."

She turned to the blackboard, where the chalk lines were still visible, etched into the dust. "Wade. Your score for today is... invalid."

I bowed deeply, keeping my head down. "Sorry for the disruption, Sensei. I will try to be quieter next time."

Chiyo-sama walked up to me, her expression uncharacteristically serious. She didn't laugh. She didn't call me a loser. She reached out and patted my shoulder, though her hands were trembling slightly from the residual shockwave.

"Soren-san," she said softly. "Even if you can't use the nice spells, that power... it felt like the stars themselves were screaming. Please, don't hide it completely. We need heroes here."

I looked up, catching her eye. For the first time since I arrived, I felt a warmth in my chest that had nothing to do with fire magic. It wasn't about conquest or glory. It was about belonging.

"I'm trying, Chiyo-san," I said, offering her a small, genuine smile. "I just want to live a quiet life."

In a world filled with monsters and demons, I had found my sanctuary. And perhaps, even a former Archdemon could learn to be a student, if he could just keep his claws sheathed.

The trees here were made of living quartz, their branches glowing with an inner light that served as the power source for the entire region. We were the last line of defense against entropy, a role that felt increasingly absurd as the world moved past our kind.

"The siphon has broken," Rinne whispered. "The blight has found the primary conduit."

"Then we move," I said, standing up. The sensation of pulling my spirit from my chest to fuel the warding spell was familiar. It hurt, but it was necessary.

We ran toward the heart of the grove. As we approached the center, the beast lunged, its clawed hands dissolving into darkness. Rinne drew her rapier, the blade humming with a fierce, chaotic energy. She was the villain, the destroyer, the force of nature unleashed, and she fought with a precision that could cut through silence.

Isolde adjusted her spectacles, which were perched precariously on her nose. “That is what they tell the children,” she said softly. “But I find that destroying things takes far more energy than fixing them. Also, the new magical enchantments require precision. My hands are steadyest when I am not running for my life.”

This artifact was the source of all high fantasy magic in the realm, and tonight, it was cracked. “We need an enchanter,” Isolde muttered, tapping her chin. “Someone who can weave threads of power without breaking them. Someone… invisible.”

“I am visible,” Jonas pointed out, crossing his arms. “I am a warrior.”

“Exactly,” Isolde smiled. “Which means you are excellent at defense, terrible at subtlety. Come. We shall attempt the ritual.”

Jonas hesitated. He was used to being the shield, the blunt instrument. Magic was something that happened to other people. But looking at the crack spreading faster, he felt a strange pull toward the orb. Not fear, but curiosity. And perhaps, duty. After all, even villains needed allies occasionally.

He moved to stand beside Isolde. She placed her hand on the cold glass surface of the gem. Her fingers began to glow, faint traces of emerald light dancing along her skin. She wasn't casting fireballs or summoning demons; she was doing something much quieter, much more difficult. She was mending reality itself.

As the mana rushed out of the gem, Isolde’s expression shifted. Her eyes closed, and sweat beaded on her forehead. The villainess persona might have been a mask for fear, but right now, it was simply concentration. She channeled her own mana, her very essence, into the crack. It was a dangerous gamble. If she failed, she would likely be consumed by the gem’s backlash. If she succeeded, the gem would stabilize, and so would the peace she claimed to despise.

“It hurts,” Isolde whispered, her voice trembling.

“Stay focused,” Jonas said, keeping his guard up not against enemies, but against the collapsing bookshelves behind them. He grabbed a heavy tome to use as a shield if the ceiling gave way. “Don’t let go, Lady Isolde.”

“I cannot!” she cried out, a tear tracing a path through the dust on her cheek. “The malice in the air… it wants to break it again! I am failing!”

The gem flared. A shockwave rippled through the room, blowing papers off shelves and rattling windows. Jonas braced himself, his muscles straining against the pressure. He watched Isolde struggle, seeing past the reputation of the wicked lady to the exhausted woman trying desperately to fix a mistake.

With a final, guttural scream, Isolde thrust her hands forward. A blinding white light erupted from the gem, expanding outward like a flower opening in slow motion. The crack vanished. The light faded. Silence returned to the library, heavier than before.

Isolde slumped against the pedestal, gasping for air. Her robes were singed at the edges, and she looked pale, almost translucent.

Jonas let out the breath he didn’t know he was holding. He walked over to her, kneeling beside her. “Are you… alright?”

I stood on the edge of the cliff, my cloak fluttering in the wind that smelled of ozone and old blood. Below me, the city was nothing more than jagged teeth poking through the earth’s crust, silent and dead.

They called her a villainess then, before she became the princess who fled. They whispered of her ambition, her pride, her refusal to bow to the King’s decree. A shadow detached itself from the treeline, vast and serpentine. It was not a bird, nor a beast of flesh and bone. It was scales, midnight blue as oil slick on water, and wings that spanned wider than the cathedral gates of the capital. A dragon. Ancient. Terrifying.

It landed softly on the stones below, its eyes glowing with a faint, inner fire. It looked up at me, tilting its massive head. There was no aggression there, only a profound, weary recognition. As if it knew exactly who I had been, and who I had become.

I should have run. Every instinct told me to flee back into the caves where I lived in obscurity, far from the politics that sought to consume us all. But the cold bit deeper than the wind. Survival demanded a price, and tonight, I decided I would pay it in gold.

The dragon lowered its snout until it was level with my eyes. A low rumble vibrated in the ground, shaking my boots. It spoke, not in words, but in emotions—curiosity, pity, and an ancient hunger for company that had long since died in the hearts of men.

"You are alone," the thought echoed in my mind, sharp and clear as breaking ice.

"I am always alone," I replied aloud, my voice steady despite the tremor in my hands. "But I am not empty."

The dragon chuckled, a sound like grinding stones. It extended a claw, each digit as thick as a man’s torso, and offered a single scale. It pulsed with warmth, alive with mana. This was a bond forged not by blood, but by necessity. A Dragon Rider. A role that had vanished from history books decades ago, dismissed as myth. Now, it was all that remained to me. If I rode this creature, I could move unseen through the mountains, deliver messages to those who defied the Crown, and perhaps, just perhaps, find a place where I could simply exist.

I took the scale. It fit perfectly in my palm, warm and solid. I closed my fingers around it, feeling the connection stir within my chest. Fear was still there, lurking at the edges of my vision, but it was drowned out by the exhilarating surge of power that rushed through my veins. This was not the sterile, controlled magic of the royal courts. This was raw, untamed, terrifyingly beautiful.

"Do you want to come with me?" the dragon asked.

The question hung in the air, heavy with implication. To accept was to sign away my anonymity forever. To ride a dragon was to become the most wanted woman in the realm, whether she liked it or not. But I looked down at the ruined city behind me, and then at the infinite, star-strewn night above. The slow life I had dreamed of was gone, replaced by something grander, more dangerous, and ultimately, more real.

"Yes," I said.

The dragon unfolded its wings, the movement displacing the ash in the air with majestic grace. It spread its limbs, creating a shelter for the lone rider standing below. With a roar that echoed off the cliffs, it took flight.

I climbed aboard, gripping the reins made of leather and hardened dragon hide. As we ascended, the lights of the city grew dim, insignificant specks beneath us. The wind whipped my hair, tearing at my cloak, but I did not care. My heart hammered against my ribs, a drumbeat of anticipation and terror. I was no longer the abandoned princess. I was not the villainess they feared.

I was a Dragon Rider, soaring into the unknown, bound to a beast of legend, leaving the past behind in the ashes of Tessaly. The horizon promised wonders and dangers beyond measure, and for the first time in years, I smiled. It was a small thing, a fragile expression on a haunted face, but it was enough. We were free. We were alive. And as the dragon dove toward the clouds, pulling me with it into the vast, indifferent beauty of the night, I knew I would never look back.

To himself, he was a ghost haunting the edges of memory, an old man with knuckles that clicked louder than a signet ring.

He adjusted the strap of his bag, the weight of the dried moonwort and silverleaf pressing against his hip. It was heavy, heavier than any plate mail he had worn in the war against the Shadow Blight. But it was honest. The leaves did not lie about their value; they simply waited to be understood.

Nils felt a jolt, not of excitement, but of recognition. He remembered when he used to brew elixirs for tired soldiers, when his hands were steady and his heart full of purpose. Now, his joints ache when the weather turns cold, and his knees grind when he walks uphill. But the magic still hummed in his veins, dormant but alive.

The journey to the Magic Academy was short. The gates were massive, carved with runes that pulsed with a soft blue light. Inside, the campus was a labyrinth of spires and gardens, vibrant with colors that hurt Nils’s aging eyes. Students hurried past, casting spells in the air, laughing, shouting, their energy bright and volatile. They didn't see the ghosts in the corridors; they only saw the future.

Nils walked alone, his footsteps echoing in the grand hall. He passed through classes filled with students practicing fireballs and lightning strikes. He saw them treat magic as a tool, a toy to be mastered. He missed the day he had treated it as a partner, something to be honored and respected.

At the door of the Herbology Department, the headmaster greeted him with a bow, though his expression remained neutral. "The professors are waiting, Sir Nils. We hope your insights will benefit our current projects."

Nils nodded. He did not need their approval anymore. He needed the truth.

Inside the laboratory, the air smelled of wet earth and decay. Shelves lined the walls with jars containing pickled mushrooms and dried roots that looked like alien organs. In the center of the room stood a cauldron bubbling with a thick, purple sludge. A student hovered over it, dropping drops of liquid from a dropper.

"It’s too viscous!" the student cried, frustrated. "The essence is rejecting the catalyst! Why won't it stabilize?"

Nils stepped forward. His heart, once beating like a drum of war, slowed to a gentle thrum. He looked at the potion, then at the student’s shaking hands. He saw the fear in the boy’s eyes—the fear of failure, the fear of inadequacy.

"Stop," Nils commanded.

The student froze, the dropper suspended mid-air.

Nils approached the cauldron. He did not touch it. Instead, he closed his eyes and listened. He could hear the heartbeat of the mana within the liquid, slow and rhythmic. It was not rejecting the catalyst; it was asking for respect. It wanted to know if its creator would care enough to listen.

He reached into his pocket and pulled out a small pouch of crushed lavender buds. With a flick of his wrist, he sprinkled them into the air above the pot. The scent filled the room, sharp and clean, cutting through the stale smell of potions.

The purple sludge rippled. Slowly, tentatively, the mixture began to settle. The foam calmed. The violent bubbling ceased. In its place, a clear, golden light emanated from the depths of the cauldron.

Silence stretched in the room. Then, the student gasped. "What... what was that?"

Nils opened his eyes. They were cloudy now, tired, but sharp. "Not just lavender," he said softly. "But the patience to wait for it to listen. Magic, like any living thing, cannot be forced. It must be invited."

Ulric adjusted his grip on the Holy Sword, a blade that hummed with a power so pure it felt like a physical weight against his palms. He stood before the obsidian dais, where the seat of power sat empty. Or rather, occupied by a figure who looked entirely too comfortable for a tyrant destined to rule the world.

This was the moment. The climax of three years of relentless training, tactical maneuvers, and spiritual alignment. Ulric was the chosen one. The Hero. The Light Bringer. And currently, he was ready to plunge his weapon into the heart of the Dark King.

The Demon Lord, known to all as Malakor the Void Weaver, was leaning back in her throne. She was small, draped in robes of deep violet silk that seemed to absorb the ambient light. Her horns were polished ivory, curved elegantly behind her ears, and her eyes—twin pools of liquid starlight—were fixed on him with an expression of profound boredom.

"So," Malakor said, her voice like velvet over gravel. "You are the one. The shiny boy in the bright armor."

Ulric took a step forward. The floorboards creaked under his boots. "I am Ulric. I have come to end your reign of terror and restore peace to the realms."

Malakor sighed. It was a long, drawn-out sound, one that echoed through the vast chamber. It wasn’t a sigh of anger. It wasn’t a sigh of despair. It was the heavy, audible exhale of someone who had just been interrupted while reading a very good book.

"Peace," she repeated, testing the word. "That is such a quaint little concept. Does it involve more naps? Because I can assure you, I am exhausted. Ruling this wretched dimension requires a lot of paperwork. The bureaucracy of evil is truly soul-crushing."

Ulric tightened his sword hilt. His knuckles turned white. This was the preamble. The monologue. In every story, the villain must explain their evil plan, why they hate humans, and how they will enslave the globe with dark magic. It was supposed to be terrifying. It was supposed to motivate the hero.

But Malakor wasn’t giving a speech. She was complaining about administrative overhead.

"Look," she continued, waving a slender hand dismissively. "The legions of shadow are fed. The mana cores are stable. If you kill me right now, the throne goes vacant. Who do you think will inherit it? Some lesser demon who probably doesn’t know how to read a budget report. Do you want to trade eternal glory for a incompetent successor?"

Ulric blinked. Once. Then twice. The adrenaline that had fueled his steps began to drain away, replaced by a creeping confusion. "You... you speak sense?"

"Sense?" Malakor raised an eyebrow. "Perhaps. Now, stop standing there looking heroic and sit down. You’re scuffing my rug."

She pointed a clawed finger toward the edge of the dais. Ulric hesitated. To sit would be an insult. To fight was absurd. He looked at his sword. It gleamed uselessly. He looked at her. She looked tired. Terribly, profoundly tired.

"If you don't mind," she added, reaching for a remote control lying on the armrest of the throne, "my manager said the annual audit arrives tomorrow morning. If I lose my footing during combat, I’ll need both hands free to hold onto my wine goblet. So please, attack efficiently and quietly. No unnecessary screaming."

Ulric felt his knees wobble. This was not how the prophecy described. The ancient texts spoke of a clash of titans, a battle for the fate of worlds. They did not mention administrative audits or noble etiquette.

"This isn't funny," Ulric muttered, though his voice lacked conviction.

"Is it?" Malakor smiled, but it didn’t reach her eyes. There was no malice there, only a strange, weary resignation. "Because if it is funny, then tell me why you came here. You could have sent a diplomat. Or maybe a lunch delivery service. I’m actually quite hungry."

The absurdity of the situation struck Ulric harder than any magical blast ever could. He lowered his sword slightly. The humming ceased, defeated by the sheer banality of the encounter. He realized then that he had been trained to defeat a monster, but never to negotiate with a overworked bureaucrat disguised as one.

The pressure in his chest, the weight of expectation and destiny, suddenly lifted. He slumped. Not dramatically, not heroically. He just sort of folded, sliding down the side of the dais until his legs gave out completely.

Malakor paused, her sip of tea mid-air. She looked down at the Hero, who was now snoring softly, his head resting on the cold stone floor.

"Well," she said, setting her cup down with a clink. "He fainted at the first sigh of my monologue. Truly pathetic. But at least he’s quiet now."

She stood up, her violet robes swirling around her ankles, and walked over to him. She picked him up, cradling him like a sack of grain.

"I suppose," she mused, walking toward a large exit marked 'Staff Only,' "we can skip the fight. Just get him to the infirmary. And check the inventory; we are critically low on high-grade sugar cubes."

As she carried the unconscious Hero out of the dark castle and into the mundane afternoon sun, the title remained true. The Hero had fallen, not to a blade, but to the sheer, unadulterated exhaustion of the world’s most powerful villain. And somewhere in the distance, the kingdom of light watched in confusion as their savior was discovered to be more of a burden than a blessing.

The salt spray tasted like iron and regret. It stung my eyes, but I refused to close them.

I am Tove, and I was supposed to be a navigator. At least, that is what the parchment scroll in my pack claimed. But looking at the jagged cliffs of the Azure Coast, where the sky met the sea in a violent, bruised purple line, I felt less like a master of tides and more like a fool walking into a cage.

High fantasy worlds are full of monsters, dragons, and ancient magic, but nothing prepares you for the crushing weight of reality when the mana starts singing. And tonight, the song wasn’t coming from the depths. It was coming from me.

"Stop," I whispered, my voice cracking over the roar of the surf. "Just stop."

I gripped the brass compass until my knuckles turned white. The needle was spinning wildly, not pointing north, but vibrating with a frantic, rhythmic pulse that matched the beat of my own heart. Now, all that remained was this small boat, half-filled with water, drifting toward the forbidden Siren’s Isle.

I looked back at the horizon. The sun was setting, bleeding gold and crimson across the waves. It was beautiful. Too beautiful. It felt like a trap.

A shadow detached itself from the mist rising off the water. It wasn’t a bird. It wasn’t a whale. It was human-shaped, yet fluid, shimmering with scales that caught the dying light.

The Siren stepped onto the bow of my boat. She wore tattered silks that drifted around her like seaweed. Her skin was pale, almost translucent, and her hair flowed behind her as if underwater, even though she stood on dry rock. But it was her eyes that stopped me. They were black voids, devoid of pupils, reflecting only the panic in my soul.

"Navigator," she said. Her voice wasn't a song. It was a whisper, cold and sharp as broken glass. "You are far from home."

"Go away," I said, though my feet wouldn’t move. "This isn't your territory."

She smiled. It was a sad, crooked thing. "Territory? There is no territory here, little one. Only us. You carried the song for weeks. I heard it. It was weak, fading. Now..." She extended a hand. "Now, I can take it back."

My breath hitched. The music started again. It wasn't coming from her lips. It was coming from inside me. A melody woven from fear and longing, the song of every sailor who had ever loved someone they couldn’t keep. It vibrated in my teeth, making my bones ache.

I remembered my father. He had sailed these seas before I was born. He had taught me how to read the stars, how to navigate by the moon’s pull. He had promised me we would build a life together, far from the dangers of the guild halls and the politics of the merchant fleets.

And he was dead. Killed by a kraken while searching for the very treasure I now sought.

That was the song. My grief. My anger. My love for him.

"If you take it," I said, tears finally streaming down my face, "what will be left?"

The Siren tilted her head. "Nothing."

"Then leave me."

She laughed, a sound like wind chimes in a gale. "Never. The song makes us eternal. But first... listen."

She began to sing.

It wasn’t a melodic tune. It was a scream. A high, piercing note that tore through the air, vibrating with such intensity that the wood of my boat splintered. I fell forward, grabbing the rail, my body jerking uncontrollably. The pain was exquisite, sharper than any blade. It felt as though my memories were being pulled out of my skull, one by one.

I saw my father laughing in a tavern. I saw my mother teaching me to tie knots. I saw the faces of my friends from the Adventurer Guild, who would mock my hesitation, who would tell me I was too soft for the harsh life of the sea.

They faded. Not slowly. Gone. Swallowed by the tide of her melody.

"No," I screamed, clutching my chest. "Stop!"

But she didn’t stop. She sang louder, pouring her power into the sound. The island seemed to groan beneath the force, the rocks shuddering. I could feel my mind unraveling, my identity dissolving into the vast, empty ocean.

Then, silence.

The song broke off abruptly, leaving a ringing void in my ears. The Siren floated closer, her face inches from mine. Her eyes were still black pits.

"Better?" she asked softly.

I tried to speak, but no words came out. I opened my mouth and found only a dull ache where my memories used to be. I remembered how to hold a rope. I remembered how to steer a rudder. I remembered the fear of drowning. But I did not remember why. I did not remember who I was.

The Siren reached out and touched my forehead. A surge of warmth flooded my veins, pulling my consciousness back into the shell of my body.

"Welcome to the sapphire seas," she murmured.

I looked up at her, really looked at her. I saw the horror in her expression for the first time. She hadn’t wanted to kill me. She had wanted to save me. To erase the burden of your loss, so you could continue sailing without the weight of grief dragging you down.

I nodded, unable to form words.

She pushed me off the bow of the boat. I tumbled into the water, gasping. The sea rose up to meet me, cool and comforting. As I swam, the memories I had lost returned, but changed. The pain was gone. In its place was a strange, hollow peace.

I just need to keep moving forward. Even if I don’t know which way is north anymore. The ocean is calling, and for the first time, I am ready to answer.

"Iris-sama," he said, bowing low. "They say you intend to stay here? To farm?"

"To live," Iris corrected him, wiping a smear of grease from her cheek. "There is a difference."

Nils smiled faintly, but his gaze drifted to the blade leaning against the wall. The sword, now sheathed, looked lonely amidst the pots and pans. "Will you ever feel that the world misses you? That the light needs your shield?"

"The light has already found its way back," Iris replied, though the words tasted bitter. "It doesn't need a hammer to stay shining. It just needs space."

Life moved slowly. It was beautiful in its simplicity, yet it felt like a slow decay of purpose. Iris spent her days tilling the stubborn soil, watching turnips sprout with agonizing slowness. In the evenings, she sat by the hearth, listening to the wind. There was no magic in the air anymore, only the scent of pine needles and damp earth.

But the peace was fragile. It felt like a thin sheet of ice over a deep, cold lake.

One afternoon, while she was gathering herbs near the forest edge, the air grew still. The birds ceased their song mid-chirp. A chill, unnatural and jagged, prickled the back of her neck. She knew that feeling. It was the same sensation that had accompanied every battle since she had taken up her holy mission.

From the trees emerged not an army, nor a beast, but a shadow. It wasn't the monstrous, towering figure of Malakor, but something smaller, more insidious. A remnant of his power, perhaps, or a manifestation of the lingering darkness that refused to die because it had lost its master.

The shadow coalesced into a woman clad in tattered, black silk. Her eyes were voids, swallowing the very light around them. She walked toward Iris, her steps silent on the moss.

"You think you can hide?" the creature whispered, its voice echoing in Iris’s skull rather than her ears. "You broke me, Hero. But what remains of us is merely the void you tried to escape."

Iris didn't draw her sword. She couldn't. The metal was too familiar, too much like the past she had buried under layers of compost and quiet routine. Instead, she reached into her pocket and pulled out a handful of seeds she had harvested from the garden—red poppies, meant for decoration, not for planting.

"Look closely," Iris said, her voice steady despite the terror clawing at her throat. "This is what remains. Not hate. Not destruction. Just life waiting to grow."

The shadow paused, tilting its head as if confused by the logic of mercy. It surged forward, claws extended to tear her apart, but before it could strike, a sudden gust of wind swept through the clearing, carrying the scent of rain and blooming flowers. The shadow flickered, its form destabilizing against the overwhelming purity of Iris’s conviction.

With a sound like tearing silk, the entity dissolved, leaving only a few scattered, glowing petals on the ground.

Iris sank to her knees, her breath coming in ragged gasps. Her hands trembled as she picked up a single red poppy. It was perfect. Unbroken.

She looked at the distant horizon, where the sun was setting in hues of orange and gold. The war was gone. The Demon Lord was dust. And though she would never truly return to the girl who once wanted to conquer the world, she had found something else. Something far more difficult, and infinitely more precious.

She stood up, brushing the dirt from her apron. The shadows would come again. The world would always find new ways to test the limits of peace. But as Iris placed the poppy gently in a vase on her windowsill, she realized that she didn't need a sword to protect this new life. She simply needed to tend it.

She smiled faintly, a small, tired expression. "Very well," she whispered to the empty space. "Since I cannot live a peaceful life in the center of the world, I suppose I shall live a very busy one here. Just not by accident."

A nap? A second cup of ale? Keep your eyes on the prize, boy! If you want to climb the ranks, you need to find something shiny! Something valuable! Something rare enough that the High Council will actually listen to you!" Milo bit his lip, his eyes darting around the crowded room. To anyone else, this was just a bustling adventurer's guild. But to Milo, it was a minefield of uselessness. In his past life, Milo had been a high school student with nothing but average grades and a knack for video games. When he woke up here, three years ago, he thought he had struck gold. His skill, Appraisal, read out stats and descriptions for every item, creature, and spell in existence. He could tell you exactly how much a goblin was worth or how much mana a sword held.

But there was a catch, a glitch in the system that drove him insane. Whenever he appraised an object with significant monetary value, or an artifact with legendary potential, the screen would simply flash: [No Value Detected.] Nothing. Zero. Even a legendary holy blade appeared as [Scrap Metal]. A shattered mirror showed [Broken glass]. A cursed relic glowing with malevolent red light displayed [Dusty Debris]. It was as if his skill was broken, a faulty lens refusing to see anything worth more than copper coins. "There you are, Milo!" Milo jumped when he heard a voice. Standing by the communal hearth was Rinna, a girl with messy twin-tails and a determined expression. She was an apprentice mage, always trying to prove herself in a guild dominated by brute strength and combat prowess. "I found this in the basement archives," she said, holding up a small, unassuming wooden box. "The previous owner discarded it because it looked 'boring.' But the guild master said it has a magical signature. Help me check it?" Milo’s heart sank. Another waste of time. Another object that would return only trash. He reached out, his fingers trembling slightly as he placed them over the lid of the box. Focus. Appraise. The world went white. Then black. Suddenly, a text box hovered in the air before his eyes. It wasn't the usual simple description. Instead, complex geometric patterns swirled within the text, shifting like water. [Object: Casket of Whispers] [Material: Unidentifiable Organic Matter] [Properties: Alters reality based on emotional resonance.] [Note: Do not open. Opening will trigger an irreversible change in your current location's temporal stability.] Milo stared. The words weren't just words; they were commands. His skill hadn't failed. It had bypassed the category of "treasure" entirely, labeling it as a hazard so dangerous it couldn't be quantified by standard market metrics. "Well?" Rinna asked, tapping her foot impatiently. "Does it have a big price tag? Does it summon dragons? Does it give us cheat skills?" Milo felt a cold sweat prickling his neck. If he told her the truth, she’d likely mock him. If he lied, he’d be stealing a ticking time bomb. He needed to get out of the guild, away from the prying eyes of Gerrick, and into the safe zone of the library. "It... it looks like it needs cleaning," Milo muttered, quickly pocketing the box before Rinna could open it. "Yes! Maybe if we polish it, it will glow brighter! Thanks, Milo!" Rinna beamed, oblivious to the fact that she was currently carrying a piece of forbidden physics into a crowded tavern. As she walked away, Milo exhaled a breath he didn't know he was holding. He sat down heavily at a corner table, pulling a menu toward himself with trembling hands. The silence of the corner was a luxury he rarely afforded himself. He watched the other adventurers—the ones who shouted about their swords and their armor—and felt a profound sense of loneliness. They saw everything in terms of combat power and profit margins. They used their skills to win fights. Milo used his skill to avoid paying taxes. Milo closed his eyes, wishing he could just disappear. But as he looked at the empty space in front of him, waiting for the next object to test his broken gift, he knew he wouldn't stop until he understood why his appraisal was the most dangerous thing in the world.

I hate Mondays.

Seriously, do these idiots not understand the power of a good weekend? I spent all Sunday practicing my death-defying aerial maneuvers in the training grounds, but now I have to face the daily grind.

Not because I want to. If only you could see how much mana I’ve been hoarding. Most knights struggle to survive the morning patrol, but I? I’m practically vibrating with pent-up energy.

"Sir Arlo, your breathing is quite heavy today," Captain Vane said, adjusting his visor. He looked like he hadn't slept since the last siege. "Are you sure you aren't overexerting yourself before the mission?"

"Relax, Captain!" I shouted back, striking a pose that was probably too dramatic for a military academy. "I am merely cultivating my inner aura! It’s called preparation for destiny!"

Vane sighed, pinching the bridge of his nose. "You are a knight in the Kingdom of Solis, not a wandering adventurer. Control yourself."

But control is boring, right? Being a high-ranking hero candidate is supposed to be exhilarating. But lately, it has been a complete disaster. Every time I tried to use my advanced magic, I ended up accidentally levitating a carrot instead of summoning a fireball.

"Hey, wait up!" I yelled, sprinting toward the main courtyard. "My quest awaits!"

It wasn't a normal quest. We were assigned to the Borderlands of Gloomreach, a territory bordering the Abyssal Rift where the Dark Forces held sway. This was supposed to be my chance to shine as the legendary warrior who would guide the kingdom into a new era of peace.

"Arlo-san! Don't run off like that!" came a tiny, frantic voice.

I slowed down, panting heavily. Standing there was a girl who looked like she had just woken up from a very bad dream. She wore tattered black lace and carried a staff that seemed far too delicate for someone commanding legions of monsters.

"Yui-sama! You shouldn't be here alone! The demon incursions are increasing!" I yelled, trying to sound heroic despite the sweat dripping down my face.

Yui sat on a cracked stone bench, looking utterly defeated. "They are coming again, Arlo-san. My father... the ruler of the Underworld... he says he must fulfill the prophecy to stabilize the rift. He feels he is failing his duty."

"What?! That's the Demon Lord!" I gasped, dropping into a low crouch. "We're supposed to stop him!"

"I know," she whispered, her eyes brimming with tears. "But he's so lonely. Even after centuries of ruling, he just wants someone to talk to. I don't know how to ask him out on a date if I'm also the wielder of eternal darkness."

I stared at her. "Is this some kind of dark joke? Is the Demon Lord actually having social anxiety?"

"He's more complicated than a monster!" she wailed. "He has a mother, he has political rivals, and he definitely has a talent for calligraphy. How can we fight him when he's clearly just misunderstood?"

Suddenly, the sky turned a sickly shade of violet. A massive shadow swept over the courtyard, and the ground began to tremble. From the rift, a squadron of obsidian-skinned beasts lunged toward us.

"They're attacking!" I screamed. "This is it! The moment I've waited for!"

I stood tall, raising my sword. "By the light of the heavens, I shall protect this realm!"

I channeled every ounce of my mana. Fireball! A wave of holy radiance! Yes!

The explosion was spectacular. It was also entirely useless. Instead of burning the monsters, the spell backfired, creating a giant, shimmering bubble around me that smelled strongly of lavender soap.

"Why is everything happening to me?!" I wailed, sliding backward on a puddle of melted mana.

The little girl, Yui, didn't look scared anymore. She looked bored.

She opened her crimson eyes and reached into her pocket. She pulled out a small, glowing orb. "Here, you idiot," she said, tossing it to me. "Use this. It's a basic demonic bind. It won't kill them, but it will keep them still so you don't die from embarrassment."

"Aha! A tactical victory!" I grabbed the orb and threw it. The monsters froze mid-pounce, stuck in a translucent jelly state.

Yui stood up, brushing dust off her skirt. "That was kind of impressive, honestly. For someone who uses magic to create scented bubbles."

I felt a blush creep up my neck. "It was... strategic hydration!"

"Whatever," she rolled her eyes. "Look, Arlo-san. The world doesn't need another war right now. My father needs a diplomatic solution. Would you come with me to the Demon Realm tomorrow? Not to slay him, but to tell him he can't just retreat to his castle every time things get difficult."

I looked at the frozen monsters. I looked at my useless, bubbly magic. Then I looked at the girl who was supposedly the daughter of the ultimate evil.

"Wait," I said, a mischievous grin spreading across my face. "If I go, does that mean we might have to share a castle? Because if I'm going to be an 'unsalvageable' part of the legend, I need to make sure my backstory is worth reading."

"Just try not to blow up any demonic temples," she warned.

"No promises!" I cheered.

As we walked away from the battlefield, I realized something. Being the chosen hero was exhausting. Being the guy who was always slightly out of sync with reality was even worse. But for the first time, being useless might actually work.

The rain in the capital city of Lunaris did not wash away the blood; it merely diluted it into a muddy slurry that clung to everything like regret. My name is Emil, and I am a knight who has failed so many times that even the stars have stopped watching me with interest. At fifty years old, my joints creak louder than a door swinging open in a drafty tavern, and my armor weighs more than a mountain goat with indigestion.

I stood at the foot of the obsidian staircase leading up to the Spire of Nyx, the seat of power for the Demon Lord Malphas. The air here smelled of ozone and burnt sugar, a cloying sweetness that promised death but delivered only disappointment. My mission was simple, or perhaps as simple as any task given to a relic of a bygone era. Deliver the treaty scrolls to the Demon Lord’s daughter, Princess Vespera, and request her hand in marriage.

I sighed, a sound lost in the drumming rain against the stone. This was my life now: a useless knight clinging to hope like a barnacle clings to a hull, while history marches on without us. Or rather, against us.

"Another one," a voice sneered from the shadows.

A group of young mages in shiny white robes emerged from behind a gargoyle. They were the Vanguard of Light, the heroes of the hour, the generation that had won the war I had fought in my youth. Their leader, a boy named Julian with hair as blonde as his arrogance, stepped forward, his sword glowing with a holy light that made my eyes water.

"Knight Emil," Julian said, his tone dripping with condescension. "We saw you coming. Did you think we wouldn’t know your pathetic presence? You’re blocking the way to the throne room."

"I am here to deliver a message," I said, my voice rough from disuse. "From the King. And from his own aging heart."

Julian laughed, a sharp, brittle sound. "The Demon Lord’s son has been missing for twenty years. His father is dead. What does a dead king want?"

"The Demon Lord is alive," I reminded him, though I knew he didn’t care about the truth. He cared about spectacle. "And she wishes to speak with you. Not to fight. To negotiate peace. For the sake of both our peoples."

Vespera was an anomaly. She was the daughter of the Demon Lord, yes, but she wore glasses and wore knit sweaters over her tail. She spent her days reading poetry in the lower dungeons, finding beauty in the darkness where others sought only terror. She did not want war. She wanted understanding.

"Let her come down," Julian spat. "Or I will chop off your head and use it as a paperweight."

My heart hammered against my ribs. It wasn’t fear. It was indignation. After fifty years of serving a kingdom that forgot its own roots, I would not be killed by some teenager playing hero in a rainy alleyway.

"You dare?" I asked, drawing my sword. The blade was rusty, chipped, and stained with old wounds. It looked less like a weapon of justice and more like a spoon used to eat soup.

Julian grinned, a predatory expression that chilled me despite the warmth of the rain. "Try it. See if that thing can cut anything but wood."

He charged.

It was a blur of motion, speed and magic. I raised my shield, expecting pain. Instead, I met a wave of kinetic energy that knocked the wind out of my lungs. I stumbled back, gasping, the impact jarring my teeth loose. But I was still standing. I had to be.

From above, a shadow detached itself from the ceiling. It wasn’t a demon beast. It was Vespera, clad in black silk, holding a scroll that glowed with soft, purple runes. Her eyes, red and fierce, locked onto mine.

"Stop," she commanded, her voice echoing with unnatural resonance.

She didn’t raise a weapon. She didn’t cast a spell. She simply looked at me, and for a moment, the rain stopped. The wind died down. Even Julian paused, confused by the sudden silence.

"Knight Emil," she said, stepping onto the balcony. "Come inside. We have much to discuss. Not about war. About peace. And about your family."

I looked at Julian, who was trembling, his holy aura flickering. Then I looked at Vespera, whose expression was not one of malice, but of profound weariness.

I sheathed my broken sword. The metal rang softly, a final note of a song ending. I bowed deeply, scraping my knees on the wet stone.

"Lead the way, Your Highness," I said.

As I walked past Julian, who watched me with wide, stunned eyes, I felt a strange sensation. Not victory, not triumph, but a quiet relief. The Demon Lord’s daughter and the useless knight. It sounded like a joke. But in the end, jokes often turn out to be the truth.

I entered the throne room. Inside, the storm raged outside, but within, there was a fire crackling in the hearth. Vespera poured two cups of tea, steamy and fragrant.

"Drink," she said. "And listen. Your story matters. More than ours."

I sat. The Demon Lord’s daughter smiled, and for the first time, I saw not a monster, but a woman trapped in a world that demanded her only hate back. And I, Emil, the useless knight, was finally the right person to hear it.

"Please don't summon me, I'm too lazy to save the world."

The words hung in the air, heavy with a sarcasm so thick you could cut it with a dull butter knife. Maren slumped further into her plush velvet chair, adjusting the silk cushions that had been tailored to support her exactly how she liked them—vertically, but comfortably numb. She stared at the crystal orb hovering before her, its surface swirling with chaotic magic and the unmistakable scent of ozone and desperation.

"You think this is a joke?" The voice came from inside the orb, deep and booming, laced with a terrifying mix of adrenaline and impending doom. It was Zeno, the Demon Lord. Or rather, what was left of him after his last failed summoning attempt. "The Barrier is cracking! The heroes are marching on the capital! We need your bloodline, your lineage, your... uh..." He coughed, trying to remember his portfolio. "...your sparkle!"

Maren closed her eyes. Her favorite tea, a rare blend of moonpetal jasmine, was getting cold. If she didn't act soon, the heat would dissipate, and she would have to spend thirty minutes reheating it. That sounded like far more work than defeating an army of demons.

"I told you," Maren said, her voice dripping with theatrical exhaustion. "I’m retired. I’m living my best slow life. The paperwork alone for saving the world is enough to give me wrinkles before my time. I haven't even worn my armor in three years."

Inside the orb, panic spiked. "You can't retire now! The prophecy says the One Who Slumbers will wake up when the Kingdom falls! That's us! Well, mostly us! I mean, the kingdom needs protecting!"

Maren sighed, a sound of profound boredom. This was the problem with being a half-dragon descendant: everyone expected you to be dramatic, powerful, and heroic. They forgot that sleep was a skill set in itself. And her current schedule involved napping, reading fiction, and avoiding responsibilities.

"Okay," she muttered, standing up. "Fine. But only if we skip the exposition. I am not listening to a ten-minute monologue about why the Dark Lord is sad. I do not have that capacity today."

The orb shimmered violently. "You’re actually agreeing? By the stars above, thank the gods and devils!"

"Don't thank the stars yet," Maren warned, pulling on her robe—a luxurious garment made of starlight thread that weighed exactly zero pounds. "I want five minutes to meditate. Then, I want snacks. Then, we fight."

This was the core of their dynamic. Zeno was a whirlwind of anxiety, energy, and magical power; Maren was a vortex of apathy and passive aggression. Yet, they were bound by blood and destiny, forced into an alliance that felt less like romance and more like a hostage negotiation where one party held all the cards and the other held all the energy drinks.

The summoning ritual began, bright lights and thunderous roars filling the room. When Maren opened her eyes, she wasn't in her cozy living room anymore. She was standing atop the highest spire of the Obsidian Citadel, surrounded by legions of shadowy minions who looked ready to charge her feet first.

Zeno appeared beside her, looking immaculate in his cape, radiating confidence that didn't quite match his sweating forehead. "Well, this is it! The battle for existence begins now!" he shouted, pointing a clawed finger toward the distant capital city below.

Maren adjusted her crown, which was slightly crooked. "Zeno, stop yelling. You're going to scare the pigeons away."

"We must maintain morale!" he declared, striking a pose. "Fear not, citizens! The Demon Lord and his... associate shall crush your arrogance!"

A group of armored knights emerged from the mists, shields raised, swords drawn. Their captain stepped forward, raising a banner that read: Justice Prevails.

Maren watched them approach, yawned widely, and then let out a soft hiss. The wind picked up, turning cold and sharp. The shadows under her cloak lengthened, detaching themselves from her body like black tendrils.

"Zeno," she said softly. "Do you have any ideas?"

"Ideas? Of course! A grand strategy! Divide and conquer! Attack from the rear! Burn the supply lines!"

"No," Maren said. "Just make them tired. And hungry."

She waved a hand casually. From the darkness behind her, hundreds of lesser demons materialized. They didn't attack the knights. Instead, they arranged themselves in a massive, chaotic circle around the battlefield, beginning to dance. It wasn't combat dancing; it was synchronized swaying accompanied by terrible singing.

The knights blinked. The captain lowered his shield, confused. "What sorcery is this?"

"It's called 'Existential Dread Dance,'" Maren explained, tapping her foot in time. "It vibrates at a frequency that causes minor nausea and profound existential fatigue. Try staying awake for this."

As the music played, the knights began to look visibly unwell. Swords clattered to the ground as men tried to find the nearest bench. Even the captain started to sway slightly, questioning his life choices.

Zeno watched in stunned silence, then burst into laughter. "This is brilliant! Pure psychological warfare! Your lazy approach worked perfectly!"

"It's just annoying," Maren corrected, stretching her arms. "Now, can we go eat? I heard there's a tavern in the lower district that serves stew. I’m starving, and if I miss lunch, I might actually start working again."

"But the world isn't saved yet!" Zeno protested, though he grinned.

"The world will survive another day without saving," Maren said, turning back toward the citadel gates with the grace of a cat walking on glass. "Come along, Hero of Doom. Let's find some food."

As they descended the spire, leaving behind the bewildered knights, Maren leaned against Zeno’s shoulder. It was warm, comforting, and smelled faintly of sulfur and victory. She closed her eyes, letting the adrenaline fade, sinking once more into the perfect bliss of doing absolutely nothing important while sitting on the edge of chaos.

But inside this hollowed vessel, the soul of Yui, once a girl with bright eyes and a stubborn heart, was slowly eroding into silence.

I sighed, a sound that rattled in a chest that had long forgotten how to breathe. My bones felt like dried leaves underfoot, brittle and tired. "Please," I whispered to the empty air. "Do not open the door. I am too lazy to save the world."

My name was Yui. Or at least, it was what the inscription on my pedestal claimed I should be called. The ritual that bound me here was supposed to summon a hero, someone brave enough to face the Demon Lord who had ravaged the continent. Instead, due to a clerical error in the summoning circle, I had been pulled out of the abyss. I hadn’t bargained for this life. I hadn’t wanted to see the end of the age. I just wanted to finish my nap.

I lifted a trembling hand, staring at my palm. The skin was pale, translucent, veined with blue shadows of fading mana. I looked up at the dark wood ceiling, where cobwebs hung thick like funeral shrouds. This was my slow life. It wasn’t peaceful; it was a suspension of death, a pause button pressed on a dying universe.

The voice boomed, rich with vitality and panic. It was Mira, the High Priestess, and by extension, the prophesied Hero. She had been sent by the kingdom, desperate to find someone with enough magical resonance to break the seal on the Demon Lord Malphas. They said I was the key. They said I was the only one left.

"But you’re the one named in the prophecy!" Mira shouted, her boots thudding against the floorboards. "Malphas is waking! The sky is turning purple! You have to come back to the castle! We need your power!"

I closed my eyes tighter. Purple skies meant chaos. Chaos meant noise. Noise meant attention. And attention was the enemy of rest. I wanted nothing more than to dissolve back into the shadows from which I came, leaving this messy, screaming world behind.

I focused my remaining strength, just enough to send a pulse of coldness toward the doors. Ice crystals formed on the lock, sealing the barrier of whatever force kept me frozen.

"Let go of the lock!" Mira screamed, but then a new sound echoed in the hall. A roar. Not human, not beast, but something ancient and hungry. The Demon Lord had arrived. The purple sky above cracked, releasing a wave of dark energy that made the dust dance violently.

Mira gasped, stumbling backward. "He’s here..."

I waited for the explosion, the clash of steel, the death screams. I waited for the world to change again. But instead of destruction, I heard something else. A whine. A pitiful, pathetic whimper coming from beneath the floorboards.

It was a creature no bigger than a kitten, with fur the color of midnight and eyes like molten gold. It was shivering, its wings tattered and broken, leaking black ichor onto the stone. It looked up at me, its tiny mouth opening in a silent plea.

It was a Imp-batling child. And it was freezing.

The Demon Lord’s laughter boomed from the top of the stairs, a sound that shook the foundations of the house. "Find us, little monster!" the voice echoed, arrogant and cruel. "And drown the hero in their own hope!"

If I died here, nothing changed. The cycle continued. The heroes would rise, the demon lords would reign, and the girl who refused to play along would fade away.

A tear traced a path through the grime on my cheek. "Lazy?" I muttered to myself. "No. Just... tired."

I dropped the bat-ling into my arms, holding it tight to my chest. The heat from its body seeped into my icy core. I stood up, ignoring the creaking of my joints. I walked past Mira, who stared at me in horror, then down at the child I held.

"What are you doing?" she hissed.

"Don't summon me," I said, my voice steadying. "I am too lazy to save the world. But I am not lazy enough to let a baby die."

The era of slowness was ending, not with a bang, but with the simple, fierce determination of a tired girl who had finally found something worth protecting.

The rain was coming down in sheets, blurring the line between the muddy path and the gray sky above. Every time I took a step, my boots sank deeper into the soil.

It was hard work. Being an apprentice to no one meant I had to do everything myself.

"Stop slouching, Sayo! Your posture is terrible for absorbing mana!"

I flinched at the shout. It wasn't Master Renji, who lived three valleys over. This was just my own voice echoing back at me in my head. Or maybe it was the wind playing tricks on my tired ears.

I sighed, adjusting the heavy satchel on my shoulder. Inside were three bundles of Moonpetal Mint and a single dried Sunberry.

My life was supposed to be exciting. That was what they said back home in the capital before... well, before the incident. Before the scandal that ruined my family name. Before I realized that being a "villainess" in someone else’s grand fantasy novel was more trouble than it was worth.

So, I ran away. I ditched my silk robes and my reputation. Now, I was just Sayo, a girl living on the edge of the known world, far beyond any kingdom’s border. A place where no one came looking for the daughter of Duke Halloway.

"Just need to get these herbs to the cottage," I muttered to myself. "Then a nice bowl of stew and a nap."

But the middle of nowhere doesn't care about your plans. The middle of nowhere cares about survival.

I rounded a sharp bend near a cluster of jagged rocks when I saw him. He was leaning against an ancient oak tree, polishing a rusted broadsword. He wore leather armor that looked like it had seen better decades, and his hair was tied back with a simple leather thong.

He looked up as I approached, and his eyes narrowed. They weren't hostile, exactly, but they were certainly judging my cheap traveling clothes and scuffed boots.

"Lost, little sprout?" he asked. His voice was gravelly, like stones grinding together.

I felt a flush creep up my neck. "No. Just passing through. Do you know if there is water nearby?"

The man scoffed. "Water? Sure. You could probably drink the puddles in those craters. But if you're asking about something potable, then yes, follow me. And watch out for the mist. It bites."

I didn't wait for an invitation. I followed him, ducking under low-hanging vines. As we walked, the sun began to dip behind the hills, casting long, violet shadows across the forest floor.

We reached a clearing dominated by a massive, crooked willow tree. At its base sat a small, stone-walled hut, smoking gently. This was my sanctuary. The herb witch’s cottage.

"Hey," I called out, pointing at the hut. "Is that empty?"

The man paused, staring at me. "It's mine."

My heart sank. "Oh. I thought..."

"It's been empty since the last adventurer died trying to dig for gold here ten years ago," he said flatly. "I just needed shelter from the storm. Why are you standing there?"

"Because I have work," I said, gripping my bag tighter. "And I haven't eaten since breakfast."

He grunted, which I took as a form of acceptance. He shuffled toward the hut, his boots crunching loudly on the dry leaves. As he entered the darkness of the porch, I noticed something glittering in the dirt near the tree trunk.

A coin. An old, tarnished copper piece. Not much, but enough for a candle.

I picked it up, feeling a surge of warmth. Even here, in this desolate corner of the map, kindness still existed.

"I'm Sayo," I called out to the figure disappearing inside. "I live here. I make tea."

There was silence. Then, a voice called back, softer this time. "Tea sounds good. Is it strong?"

"Stronger than anything you've ever tasted," I promised.

I hurried to the kitchen area—a modest room with a hearth and a workbench covered in vials and dried leaves. I grabbed my kettle and started the fire. As the water began to boil, I arranged the ingredients. Rosemary for the clarity, lavender for the calm, and a touch of crushed chamomile to sweeten the bitterness of my past.

When I served him a cup, steam curling around his face, he took a long sip. His shoulders relaxed slightly. The tension in his jaw eased.

"It's... decent," he admitted.

"It's herbal infusion," I corrected gently. "Not magic. Magic requires intent. This is just plant science."

He chuckled, a dry sound. "Plant science. You sound like a scholar. Where did you come from?"

I looked out the window. The rain had stopped, leaving the world washed clean and quiet. No armies were marching. No poison ivy was sent by jealous nobles. Just me, the herbs, and the silence.

"From somewhere loud," I said softly.

He stared into his mug. "Good. Loud is exhausting."

We stayed in companionable silence for a while longer. He told me about a lost trail; I told him how to identify a nightshade berry without touching it. We were strangers sharing a campfire and a meal, but for the first time in months, I felt grounded. Rooted.

As night fell, he eventually stood up. "Thanks for the tea, Sayo. Stay safe."

"You too," I replied, waving as he stepped back into the dark woods.

I watched him go until he vanished into the shadows. Then, I turned back to my hearth. My hands were tired, my feet were sore, and tomorrow would bring new challenges. There would be monsters in the caves and diseases in the swamps. But as I dried the mugs and set my tools in order, I smiled.

This was my life now. Slow. Quiet. Mine.

And for a villainess who spent her youth fighting battles she never wanted to fight, it was exactly what I needed.

I stood up too. My boots clicked on the wooden floor. I didn’t run toward the fear. I ran toward the gears.

I threw the Tuner onto the ground near the heart of the beast. The moment it landed, the gears began to spin, driven by a spring mechanism I had pre-wound. The copper wires hummed, emitting a low-frequency vibration that resonated with the earth itself.

"Magic is just another way to move things," I said, wiping sweat from my forehead. "This... this was engineering."

She reached out, touching my shoulder. Her touch was warm, despite her exhaustion. For the first time in years, the tension in her shoulders dropped.

"Thank you, Rin," she said, her voice cracking.

I smiled, a small, tired thing. "Don't thank me. Fix your wand. We have work to do."

The voice that broke my trance was not menacing; it was profoundly bored. I blinked, the dust motes dancing in the shaft of sunlight hitting my eyes like tiny, judgmental spectators. Sitting on the edge of the fountain in the center of the bustling marketplace was Milo, the self-proclaimed guardian of the city’s peace and quiet. He was currently polishing a sword that looked suspiciously like a kitchen utensil wrapped in shiny cloth.

I am Nadia, former Knight-Commander of the Iron Rose Legion, retired due to a knee injury and an unwillingness to march anymore. Now, I run the best bakery in Brindle, which is roughly translated to: I make pastries.

"Your blade looks dull, Milo," I said, adjusting my apron. Flour dusted my cheekbones, which I hadn’t realized were still there.

He stopped polishing. "It is high-maintenance stuff. You wouldn’t understand, Nadia. You only know how to knead dough. Where is the glory? Where is the thrill of battle?"

"There is no battle today, unless you count the struggle of keeping these scones from burning," I replied, stepping out from behind the counter. The sun felt warm on my skin. This was my life now. High Fantasy, yes, but low stress. That was the slogan on the wall.

Milo sighed, tossing the polishing rag aside. "The rumors say the Shadow Beasts are gathering near the Whispering Woods. The King demands more warriors."

I raised an eyebrow, holding up a tray of golden-brown rolls. "And I demand they stop calling me 'Sir Tough.' My name is Nadia. Sir Tough is what happens when you drop your gear during a dust storm. Do you want one of these?"

"I do," he said, grabbing one with surprising dexterity for a man who refused to sharpen his weapons. "Eat something, adventurer. You look like you haven't slept since the last war ended."

I took a bite. It was warm, buttery, and perfect. In that moment, the heavy weight of expectation that had crushed me decades ago lifted slightly. I had fought dragons. I had buried friends. I had won battles that changed the course of history. But here, serving coffee to a boy obsessed with swords, I found something else. Peace.

However, the peace shattered exactly three minutes later.

A shadow fell over the awning, thick and unnatural. The birds stopped singing. The chatter of the market died instantly. From the alleyway emerged not a Shadow Beast, but Lord Vane, the Duke’s cousin, who had a reputation for being cruel, boring, and terrible at diplomacy. He held a single, withered rose.

"Nadia," he sneered. "You have been hiding in this filth for too long. Come with me. The King needs your... 'unique talents.'"

Milo stepped forward, clutching his unpolished sword. "We don't need him! We need silence!"

Lord Vane ignored them, focusing his cold eyes on me. "The rumors about your strength are true. I wish to test you. A duel. One life. For the honor of the Realm."

The crowd gasped. The low hum of the bakery went silent. Even the oven seemed to hold its breath.

My heart hammered against my ribs, not with fear, but with memory. Years ago, Vane had orchestrated the ambush that cost my squad their legs. I had retreated, believing myself broken. But looking at Vane now, frail and pathetic in his arrogance, I felt no rage. Only pity. And also, extreme hunger.

I looked at Milo. He nodded, though he didn’t understand why. Then I looked at the crowd. They wanted spectacle. They wanted heroism. They expected me to draw my sword and cry about loss.

Instead, I took another bite of the scone.

"Lord Vane," I said, my voice calm and clear. "You wish to duel? Very well. But we must adhere to the rules of engagement."

Vane frowned. "Rules? What rules?"

"Hygiene," I said, pointing to the open street. "And manners. You track mud everywhere. It ruins the floorboards."

He sputtered, ready to retort, but I wasn’t done. I placed my hand on the counter, right next to the display case containing the day’s most delicate creation: a dozen emerald macarons, baked with special herbs that smelled faintly of mint and rain.

"These macarons," I continued, lifting one by one, "are crafted with the finest sugar and butter. If you attack this place, you attack my livelihood. And if you destroy my livelihood, you insult the craft itself."

Vane hesitated. He looked at the cookies, then at me. The absurdity of the situation hung in the air, thicker than the flour dust. He looked ridiculous. A warrior seeking death by pastry.

"What?" he demanded.

"I said, no fighting," I said softly. "Just leave. Go back to your dungeon. Think about what you’ve lost. Not just the titles, but the respect. Because today, you have none of that."

Vane stared at me, speechless. For a moment, the high tension crackled between us, electric and sharp. Then, with a huff of indignant steam, he turned on his heel and stomped away, muttering about incompetence and sugary traitors.

Silence returned. Not the tense, expectant silence before the storm, but a relaxed, satisfied silence.

Milo let out a long breath. "That... that was anticlimactic."

I smiled, wiping my hands on my apron. "Better than dragging my sword. Besides, the aroma of fresh baking is far more intoxicating than the scent of blood and betrayal."

I picked up the tray of macarons. "Now, help me pack these up. The customers are hungry."

Milo grinned, reaching for his sword again. "You know, sometimes I think you’re secretly a sorceress."

"I’m a baker," I corrected him gently. "With a good knee, I can lift anything."

As I walked around the counter, surrounded by the smells of cinnamon and comfort, I realized that while the world would never understand the nuances of my victory, it didn't matter. I was safe. I was happy. And I had a mountain of delicious work ahead of me.

Being the Emerald Hero wasn't about slaying monsters. It was about baking the world a better tomorrow, one perfectly crisp cookie at a time.

"Stop right there, you overgrown moss-beast! Or do you prefer to be flattened by a hero’s legendary strike?"

The voice was sharp, ringing with the confidence of someone who had never once met a failure. Arlo gripped the hilt of his blade, his knuckles turning white. Sweat stung his eyes, not from fear, but from the sheer adrenaline coursing through his veins like liquid fire. Behind him, Kaelen gasped, clutching her side. The air smelled of damp earth and rotting vegetation, thick enough to choke a man.

Arlo was nothing. Just a boy with no lineage, no magic, and no reputation. Yet here he stood, staring down the massive, shifting form of the Grotto Warden—a creature that had swallowed three villages whole before he even found it.

"I am not your enemy," the beast rumbled, its voice shaking the ground beneath their feet. "I am merely protecting the Root of Ages. Leave, little human, and I will let you die in peace."

"Peace is boring!" Arlo shouted, stepping forward. He ignored the pain in his lungs and the terror whispering in the back of his mind. To quit now would mean becoming the weakling everyone expected him to be. He would never be more than background noise again. Not today. Today, he would rewrite the script.

He drew his sword, the steel reflecting the dim green glow of the cavern walls. It wasn't the polished, enchanted steel of the knights in the capital. It was simple, forged in a local smithy, but it hummed with something else. Something ancient. He didn't know why, but when he held it, he felt connected to the very lifeblood of the forest itself.

Kaelen coughed, trying to stand. "Arlo, wait! That thing is ancient. Its hide is harder than diamond. You can’t scratch it."

"Let me try," Arlo said. His voice was steady now, fueled by a hot-blooded determination that burned brighter than any spell. He closed his eyes for a second, feeling the pulse of the world. Deep roots, swirling water, the slow, heavy beat of the heart of the forest. It wasn't magic in the flashy sense—no sparkles, no chanting. It was a raw, primal energy that Arlo had somehow unlocked within himself.

He opened his eyes and lunged.

The Warden swung a colossal fist made of hardened bark and stone. Arlo ducked, the wind of the blow whipping past his ears so violently he felt his hair lift. Time seemed to slow down. In this moment, everything existed in perfect clarity. The cracks in the Warden’s armor were visible. The rhythm of its breathing was audible. The trajectory of the swing was predictable.

This is it, Arlo thought, a grin spreading across his face despite the danger. This is the climax! This is where the underdog shines!

He sprinted toward the beast’s legs, dodging another sweeping tail made of living vines. The impact shook him to the bone, but Arlo rolled, using the momentum to slide under the limb. He was close. Too close. But he wouldn't pull back.

With a roar that tore from his throat, he drove his sword upward. He didn't aim for the tough, armored carapace. Instead, he sought the glowing core visible near the Warden’s neck, pulsing with emerald light—the source of its power.

Clang!

The impact sent a shockwave up Arlo’s arms, nearly shattering his elbows. Pain exploded in his body, blinding and intense, but Arlo pushed through it. He channeled every ounce of his will, every dream of becoming the greatest adventurer in the realm, into that single point.

"Die!" Arlo screamed, throwing his entire weight into the thrust.

The blade pierced the glowing node. For a heartbeat, there was silence. Then, the emerald light flared, blindingly bright, filling the cavern with a surge of vibrant green energy. The Warden froze, its massive form convulsing. With a final, shuddering groan, the giant collapsed, dissolving into mist and leaves that rained softly onto the floor like confetti.

Silence returned to the grotto.

Arlo fell to his knees, gasping for air. Blood trickled from his nose and mouth, coating his teeth. He looked up to see Kaelen rushing over, tears streaming down her face.

"Arlo... you actually did it," she whispered, her voice trembling. "You killed the Guardian of the Roots..."

Arlo wiped his mouth with his sleeve, wincing at the ache in his ribs. He looked at his hands, still gripping the hilt of his modest sword. They weren't the hands of a mage or a knight. They were the hands of a survivor.

"Of course I did," Arlo said, a fierce, triumphant smile breaking through his exhaustion. He stood up, his legs unsteady but his spirit unbroken. "A hero doesn't wait for permission. A hero takes what belongs to them."

Outside, the sun began to set, casting long shadows over the forest. The path ahead was dangerous, filled with unknown monsters and darker mysteries, but as Arlo sheathed his blade and took his first step out of the ruins, he felt a warmth in his chest that had nothing to do with physical strength.

He was no longer just a boy hiding in the shadows. He was the one who had faced the impossible and won. The stories would change tomorrow. By dawn, they would call him many things—Hero, Savior, Victor.

But tonight, under the emerald light of the forest, Arlo knew one thing with absolute certainty. He was going to be great. And he would burn every obstacle in his way to make sure of it.

"I refuse to wear that frilly lace."

The words hung in the air of the Grand Hall of the Tessaly Magic Academy, thick enough to cut with a blade. Pia did not turn around. She sat upon the cold marble steps outside the massive oak doors, her back straight, chin slightly raised. Her eyes remained fixed on the distant, jagged peaks of the Blackspine Mountains, where the clouds swirled like bruised flesh.

Inside, the murmurs had ceased. The Headmaster’s voice, usually booming and authoritative, now trembled with a desperate kind of fear.

"Pia von Hellsing," the Headmaster began, his hands shaking as he gestured toward the empty spot beside him. "You have been stripped of your rank as Archmage Candidate. You have been banished from the academy grounds until such time as you demonstrate... rehabilitation."

Pia finally looked up. Her face was pale, but her eyes burned with a quiet, terrifying intensity. "Rehabilitation? For what?"

"For your behavior," cried out Lady Zeno, a noblewoman whose hair was perfectly coiffed and whose heart was full of venom. "The rumors are true, girl! You manipulated the mana currents during the midterm exam. You sabotaged our elemental resonance circles! You are a wicked lady, a blight upon this institution!"

A gasp rippled through the crowd of students and faculty. To be called a 'wicked lady' here meant more than social ruin; it meant they were marking her as a threat, an enemy of the state sanctioned by the academy itself. In this dark fantasy world, magic was power, and she had been branded as wielding it too dangerously.

"I used the ancient runes to stabilize the overflow," Pia said softly. "Your theory failed because your mana flow was erratic. I merely corrected the error."

"You cheated!" shouted a boy named Jiro, a popular student who had never looked her way. He pointed a trembling finger. "I saw you casting those forbidden shadows! You’re a monster!"

Pia closed her eyes. She felt the weight of their judgment, the cold stone beneath her fingers, the humiliation burning in her cheeks. But underneath the shame, something else was stirring. Something vast. Something hungry.

She reached into the folds of her cloak, pulling out a small, obsidian pendant shaped like a dragon’s head. It pulsed with a dull, rhythmic throb against her palm. This was no ordinary trinket. It was a tether. A bond forged in blood and starlight.

"Before you cast me out," Pia whispered, her voice barely audible over the rising panic in the room, "know this: when you call me a monster, you do not understand what I am."

She opened the pendant.

The shadows in the corner of the hall lengthened, twisting into serpentine shapes that writhed across the floor. The temperature dropped instantly, frost creeping along the windowpanes. The chandeliers flickered and died, plunging the Grand Hall into darkness save for the eerie, violet glow emanating from the pendant.

From the shadow beneath Pia’s feet, a roar erupted—not sound, but pure pressure. It hit the gathered nobles like a physical blow, knocking several unconscious. The air screamed. The very stones of the academy groaned under an invisible force.

Then, a figure manifested.

It was immense, composed of smoke and starlight, with scales that shimmered like polished gemstones. Eyes like molten gold opened within the abyss of its form, fixing on every person in the room. It was not human. It was the Dragon King of the Abyss, imprisoned within the vessel of Pia’s spirit for centuries.

He rose from the darkness, his presence crushing the will of everyone present. He stepped forward, the ground cracking with each movement. He looked down at the terrified students, then at the horrified faculty. His gaze was ancient, devoid of mercy, yet strangely protective of the girl kneeling before him.

"Lords and Ladies of Tessaly," the Dragon King’s voice echoed directly in their minds, bypassing their ears entirely. It was deep, resonant, and utterly commanding. "You speak of wickedness. You speak of cheating. Yet you bind yourself to this academy by oaths sworn in truth. Do you deny your own hypocrisy?"

Lady Zeno fell to her knees, weeping. "Monster! Wretch! Burn them!"

The Dragon King turned his golden eyes toward the lady. "Burn?" He tilted his head, a gesture of immense power restrained by politeness. "I find fire rather pedestrian. But perhaps... I might suggest another method. Ones that require less mess."

Pia stood up, brushing the dust from her skirt. The tension in the room was suffocating, a heavy blanket of dread. She felt the familiar warmth of the Abyss pressing against her mind, a soothing counterpoint to the terror.

"My familiar says he is offended by your insults," Pia said, stepping past the paralyzed Headmaster. She walked toward the heavy doors, ignoring the gasps and the whispers. "And also that he requires fresh ozone after being held in stale mana for three years."

As she passed the threshold, the Dragon King bowed deeply, a gesture of respect toward his mistress. The oppressive aura lifted slightly, replaced by a lingering scent of sulfur and ozone.

Pia stepped out into the twilight. The sky above the academy was darkening, a bruise of purple and black. She didn't look back at the doors. She knew they would remain shut behind her. They had cast her out, yes. But they had forgotten one crucial detail about the woman who had just left: she was no longer merely a student.

She was the daughter of the Abyss. And the world was about to learn how to tremble.
